::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[finding f'(x) of a parametric integral function without evaluating it](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2465273/finding-fx-of-a-parametric-integral-function-without-evaluating-it), asked by [K.T.](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/489633/k-t) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-10-10; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> >$$f(x)=\int_0^x \sqrt{1-sin(\pi t)} dt$$
> Find $f'(x)$ without doing the integral.
>
> I tried using the fundamental law of calculus with the inner function as $g(t)$
> and evaluated it to $f'(x)= \frac d{dx} (G(x)-G(0))$ but I don't think I can do that without first evaluating the integral.
:::

>I tried using the fundamental law of calculus with the inner function as $g(t)$
and evaluated it to $f'(x)= \frac d{dx} (G(x)-G(0))$ but I don't think I can do that without first evaluating the integral.

What is $G(x)$?  I presume you mean, an antiderivative of $g(x)$.  If $G$ is an antiderivative of $g$, what would $\frac{d}{dx}G(x)$ be?
